issues.legal_issue: A legislature may validate past actions that a court has held invalid without thereby exercising judicial power, provided the validating law is within its legislative competence and complies with constitutional limitations.
material_facts: A prior Supreme Court decision had held that a single acquisition notification could not support successive declarations covering different parcels of land.

Parliament enacted a law declaring that past acquisitions and related actions would not be invalid merely because more than one report or declaration had been made under the same notification, notwithstanding contrary court orders.
The law concerned land acquisition, a subject within Parliament's legislative competence.
issues.conclusion: The validating law did not encroach on judicial power and was not invalid merely because it affected actions previously held invalid by a court.
issues.legal_principle: The Indian Constitution does not apply the American doctrine of a strict separation of legislative and judicial powers. Legislative power to validate actions is ancillary to the power to legislate on the relevant subject, but remains subject to the constitutional distribution of legislative authority and fundamental rights. The Court relied on A.K. Gopalan v. State, The Queen v. Burah, United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum, Piare Dusadh v. The King Emperor, Basanta Chandra Ghose v. King Emperor, and West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validating_l: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law that validates past actions.
predicates.prior_court_ruling_invalidated_the_actio: A court had previously held the relevant actions invalid.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_the_subje: The legislature that enacted the validating law had authority to legislate on the subject of those actions.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a validating law, a prior ruling invalidating the actions and legislative authority over their subject do not, by themselves, make the validating law invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A law may validate acquisitions made under an earlier notification despite not giving retrospective effect to amendments that authorize multiple reports and declarations.
material_facts: The earlier acquisition notification had been followed by a first declaration and then by further declarations for other parcels of land.
Under the earlier Supreme Court ruling, those later declarations could not be supported by the original notification.
The validating law provided that acquisitions and related actions would not be invalid merely because multiple declarations had been made under one notification, notwithstanding contrary judgments.
The amendments authorizing multiple reports and declarations were not expressly made retrospective.
issues.conclusion: The absence of express retrospective operation for the amendments did not invalidate the separate provision validating past acquisitions and actions.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may validate past actions either by expressly making an amendment retrospective or by separately providing that past actions are not to be treated as invalid on specified grounds. The power to enact the latter form of validation is ancillary to legislative power over the subject, subject to constitutional limitations. The Court relied on United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum, Piare Dusadh v. The King Emperor, and West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validation_o: A party challenges a law that validates past land acquisitions.
predicates.one_notification_was_followed_by_multipl: The acquiring authority made more than one declaration concerning parcels covered by the same earlier notification.
predicates.validation_law_expressly_preserves_past_: The legislature expressly provided that past acquisitions and related actions would not be invalid on the specified ground.
predicates.underlying_amendment_is_not_expressly_re: The amendment authorizing the relevant procedure was not expressly given retrospective effect.

issues.definition: Past acquisitions are not invalid merely because a procedural amendment is prospective when a validating law expressly preserves those past actions.

issues.legal_issue: Validating later parcel-by-parcel acquisitions under an earlier notification does not violate the constitutional guarantee concerning compensation when the governing compensation principles remain unchanged and the notification date remains relevant to valuation.
material_facts: The acquisitions were made for the same public purpose stated in the original notification.
The law validated multiple declarations for different parcels under that notification and did not expressly change the compensation provisions or the principles for determining compensation.
The existing acquisition law used the value prevailing at the notification date as the basis for valuation.
The acquisition concerned a large planned development that the State could not necessarily undertake all at once because of planning and resource constraints.
issues.conclusion: The validating law did not violate the constitutional guarantee concerning compensation.
issues.legal_principle: After the constitutional amendment of 1955, the adequacy of compensation is not justiciable, but the law must provide compensation or principles for determining it. The Court considered the existing notification-date valuation principle relevant and found that validation of successive declarations did not introduce a different public purpose or alter the compensation principle. Sections 4 and 23 of the Land Acquisition Act were protected by Article 31(5)(a), while the amendments concerned the procedure for reports and declarations. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, and P.V. Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compensation: A party challenges the constitutionality of compensation in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.successive_parcels_serve_the_same_public: The parcels acquired through successive steps serve the same public purpose identified for the acquisition.
predicates.existing_compensation_principles_are_unc: The validating law does not alter the existing principles for determining compensation.
predicates.notification_date_is_relevant_to_the_acq: The date used to value the property is connected to the commencement of the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.phased_acquisition_is_consistent_with_pl: The acquisition is carried out in stages for reasons connected with planning or the State's available resources.

issues.definition: Validation of successive acquisitions does not violate the compensation guarantee when the parcels serve the same purpose, the existing compensation principles remain unchanged, the valuation date is connected to the acquisition, and phased acquisition is consistent with planning or available resources.

issues.legal_issue: Different treatment of acquisitions depending on whether the relevant notification preceded or followed the law's commencement, and whether compensation had already been received, does not by itself violate equal protection when the classifications are rationally related to the law's objectives.
material_facts: The law set different deadlines for declarations depending on whether the acquisition notification was issued before or after the specified commencement date.
The law provided interest in certain delayed acquisitions but excluded acquisitions for which compensation had already been paid.
The law addressed both pending acquisitions and future acquisitions, including delays in completing acquisition proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The challenged distinctions did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equal protection.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not prohibit every difference in treatment created by an amending law, including differences between completed and future transactions. A classification is permissible when it is intelligible and rationally related to the law's objective. The Court relied on Jalan Trading Co. v. Mazdoor Union and Hatisingh Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge_to_acq: A party challenges acquisition rules as denying equal protection.
predicates.law_distinguishes_by_when_proceedings_be: The law treats proceedings differently according to when they began or whether compensation had already been paid.
predicates.the_distinguished_groups_are_not_similar: The groups differ in circumstances relevant to the law's objective, or the distinction bears a rational relation to that objective.

issues.definition: A distinction based on the timing or completion of acquisition proceedings does not deny equal protection when the groups are not similarly situated or the distinction is rationally related to the law's objective.

issues.legal_issue: Different treatment of a proposed development that had not obtained approval of both its layout and service plans before acquisition proceedings is not discriminatory when the authorities released only developments that had obtained both approvals.
material_facts: Authorities released certain developments from acquisition when both their layout plans and service plans had been approved before the acquisition notification.
The affected owner's layout plan had been approved, but the service plans had not been approved before that notification.
The owner's development plans also faced unresolved questions concerning proof of ownership of some parcels.
issues.conclusion: The owner's land had not been subjected to unconstitutional discrimination because it did not meet the criteria applied to the developments that were released.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a distinction supported by a consistent policy and relevant differences in the circumstances of the affected properties. The Court found that the release policy depended on prior approval of both layout and service plans and that the affected development did not meet that criterion.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge_to_dif: An owner challenges different treatment of land in an acquisition proceeding as discriminatory.
predicates.authorities_released_only_developments_w: The authorities' release policy required both development plans to have been approved before the acquisition notification.
predicates.the_challenged_development_lacked_one_or: The challenged development had not obtained all approvals required by the policy before the acquisition notification.

issues.definition: Different treatment is not discriminatory when the authorities release only developments meeting a prior-approval criterion and the challenged development did not meet that criterion.

issues.legal_issue: A validating law that preserves acquisitions based on an exhausted notification, without reviving that notification or providing a legislative basis for the later acquisitions, impermissibly fixes compensation by reference to an anterior valuation date.
material_facts: A first declaration had been made for part of the land covered by an earlier notification, after which the notification was exhausted under the prior Supreme Court ruling.

The validating law purported to preserve later acquisitions and declarations based on that notification but did not retrospectively amend the relevant provisions or otherwise revive the exhausted notification.

The later acquisitions could therefore proceed without a fresh notification, and compensation would continue to be based on the value at the date of the exhausted notification despite intervening appreciation in land values.
issues.conclusion: The dissenting judges would have held the validating provision invalid because it both failed to revive the exhausted notification and derogated from the constitutional compensation guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: In the dissent's view, the constitutional requirement of compensation continued to require a just equivalent, even though adequacy itself was not reviewable. A law that in substance fixes compensation by reference to a date unconnected to the later acquisition, while omitting a legislative provision to revive the exhausted notification, fails that requirement. The dissent relied on State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector, and Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validation_o: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law validating land acquisitions.
predicates.earlier_notification_was_exhausted_after: A prior declaration acquired part of the land and, under the governing interpretation, exhausted the notification for the remaining land.
predicates.validation_does_not_legislatively_revive: The validating law preserves later actions without providing a legislative basis that revives the exhausted notification.
predicates.later_acquisitions_use_the_old_valuation: Later acquisitions rely on the valuation date of the exhausted notification despite appreciation in the property's value before those acquisitions.

issues.definition: Under the dissent's approach, the validating provision is invalid when it preserves later acquisitions without reviving the exhausted notification and thereby uses an earlier valuation date despite intervening appreciation.
